title: I redesigned my whole mobile game with an image model – the hard part wasn't the concepts, it was turning them into something that runs on old phones
author: thexyba
selftext:
I'm a solo dev working on **Scitch**, a live reaction game for Android and iOS (up to 24 players per round, the slowest get knocked out). Over the last weeks I redesigned the entire app, and I wanted to share how the AI part actually worked, because it was different from what I expected.

The image shows one screen, the matchmaking lobby, from start to finish.

**1. Concepts: references beat clever prompts**

My first concept prompts without references gave me beautiful screens that had nothing to do with my game. What worked was feeding the image model (Nano Banana Pro) the *current* screenshots plus the logo, a few avatars and boss characters, and asking for an "evolution of the current app, same layout". From there I iterated per screen.

Things that kept going wrong and needed explicit rules in the prompt:

* the logo got redrawn every time, so it got its own reference image and a "logo rule" paragraph
* it loved adding emoji-style icons and random robots as players, I had to forbid both and pass my real avatar sheet
* header elements drifted between screens until I wrote one fixed "header rule" block that I prepend to every prompt

**2. A concept is not an asset**

A concept image is one flat picture with baked-in text and fake UI. You can't ship that. So for each screen I went back and generated the parts separately: an empty arena, the glass jar, a separate front layer with just the glass glare, a blank rank shield in neutral silver (tinted to bronze/silver/gold in code), a calendar orb with an empty page so the date can come from the app. Everything is generated on flat green or magenta and keyed out with a small Python script.

The lobby jar is the best example: back layer (jar + arena), then the player balls animated live in Flutter, then the glass glare on top. Looks like the balls are *inside* the glass, but it's just three layers.

**3. Pre-rendered instead of live effects**

The concepts are full of glow, glass and blur. Doing that live in Flutter (blur filters, masks, opacity stacks) was too heavy on older Android phones. So every glow, every glass highlight and every pedestal is a finished image now. No runtime blur at all. It also made the look much more consistent, because the "material" comes from the same model and style rules everywhere.

**4. Building it**

The UI code was written with an AI coding assistant (Claude Code). My loop was: put the concept and a simulator screenshot side by side, list what's off ("ring too thin", "balls fall through the glass instead of into it"), fix, repeat. That comparison step is where most of the time went, and it's the part I wouldn't hand off.

**What I'd do differently:** write the style rules down *before* generating the first concept. I ended up with a one-page style guide (near-black background, one main color with a rim glow, highlight top left, everything built from balls, no text in images) and every asset after that needed far fewer retries.

The new design ships with the next update of the open beta. If you're curious how it plays: scitch.com

**Question for you:** how do you get from AI concept art to real, layered game assets? Do you regenerate parts like I did, or paint over the concept by hand?

*Disclosure: Scitch is free to play with an optional cosmetics shop. The game itself doesn't use AI at runtime. AI was used for the art (Nano Banana Pro), parts of the code (Claude Code) and music (Lyria).*
